The larger diameter fibers are the glass fibers (in green) and the smaller diameter are the carbon fibers (in yellow) Figure 66 and 67 shows the flexural strength and flexural modulus for the variants shown in Table 7. The dashed line in the figure is commercial 20 wt% glass fiber standard purpose SMC from IDI Composites, Noblesville, Indiana. The specimens were tested both in the MD (X) and CD (Y) respectively. A couple of trends were noted from these tests: For all variants the MD was from ~4 to 18% higher than the CD. For the 2/19-PI specimen the glass fiber side was on the tensile side of the flexural loading. These samples showed highest 49 values on flexural strength, 244 MPa (MD) and 187 MPa (CD). For the 2/26-P2 and P4 the rCF was on the tensile side. The single charge 2/26 P2 exhibited ~18% lower flexural strength in the MD and 10% lower in the CD. The two charge 2/26 P4 had ~40% lower flexural strength (149 MPa) versus the 244 MPa for the single charge 2/19 P1 and 39% lower strength for the 2/26-P2 (149.3 MPa). The three charge 3/05-P2 had 38% lower flexural strength than the 2/19- P1. The 2/26 and 3/05 samples were very comparable in performance. Similar trends were observed for the flexural modulus as shown in Figure 67. The flexural strengths of the hybrid SMC produced were very comparable and in many cases exceeded those of commercial SMC. In all cases the flexural modulus of the hybrid SMC was 12-40% lower than commercial SMC. Note: All specimens were tested with CF on the bottom side, expect 2/19 P1 where glass fiber was on the bottom side. Figure 66.Comparison of flexural strength (MPa) for the hybrid SMC variants listed in Table 6. Several insights were gained from these studies. The higher performance of the hybrid SMC when loaded from the carbon side with glass on the bottom (2/19 P1) can be attributed to longer glass fibers (1”) and their network acting more like continuous bridging fibers.
